title: AI-assisted key art, custom pixel art: what I learned building a cozy idle game
author: MasterSteak4510
selftext:
I'm building Idle Roasters, a cozy pixel-art idle game. I used generative AI for the store key art, but deliberately kept the in-game pixel art and code custom. Here's the boundary and what I learned.



What AI did:

\- Store key art: Gemini scene, composited with a custom IDLE ROASTERS pixel wordmark.

\- Music: Suno-generated tracks by UIT GAMES (licensed).

\- No AI-generated in-game sprites. The 9 location scenes and 35 actor sprites are generated by a custom Python pixel-art pipeline with fixed layout constraints.



Why:

The in-game art has to fit a 250×110 scene card, actor walk lanes, a counter foreground region, and day/night variants. Generative images looked great as key art but were not reliable for that grid. The custom pipeline gave me consistent sprites and fast iteration.



What I learned:

\- AI key art is fast; compositing and typography are where the work is.

\- A procedural pixel-art pipeline is not "less work"; it's a different kind of work.

\- Players judge the in-game look, not the store art. The boundary matters.



The free demo is 5–15 minutes. The full version has 9 locations, 60 achievements, a Time Machine, Legacy Shares, and two endings.



Demo: [https://juba13.itch.io/idle-roasters](https://juba13.itch.io/idle-roasters)

Full: [https://juba13.itch.io/idle-roasters-full](https://juba13.itch.io/idle-roasters-full)



I'm the developer; the full version is paid, so this is commercial self-promo. I'd love feedback on the AI/non-AI boundary and how the store art compares to the in-game art.



What would you have done differently?
